chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man: is it permissible for him to marry a woman with whom he had illicit relations? He said, 'If he perceives maturity/reasonableness in her, then yes; otherwise, let him tempt her into illicit relations; if she continues with him, she becomes forbidden to him; if she refuses, let him marry her.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And there is no harm for a man to marry a woman whose mother or daughter he had intercourse with; the marriage of the mother and daughter is not forbidden to him, whether the intercourse was before the contract as we clarified, or after it, in any case. (1350) 8. The one who mentioned it narrated - Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hashim ibn al-Muthanna who said: I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when a man asked him, 'A man had illicit relations with a woman; is her daughter permissible for him?' He said, 'Yes, indeed, the forbidden act does not invalidate the permissible.'

key_terms.يَفْجُرُ بِهَا: He had illicit sexual relations with her

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a man to marry a woman he previously had illicit relations with, and does it affect her mother or daughter?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the principle that *al-haram* (illicit intercourse) does not invalidate *al-halal* (marriage), a key concept in Shia jurisprudence distinguishing between temporary illicit relations and permanent marital bonds. The primary narration offers a pragmatic approach where the man may either marry directly if he perceives her suitability or engage in further relations to solidify the bond, while the secondary narration explicitly permits marrying the mother or daughter of the woman he had relations with, confirming that the prohibition is specific to the individual and not her close female relatives. This ruling underscores the flexibility of *nikah* in removing the barrier of *fujur*, provided the woman is not his direct mahram.
